paper_title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

Introduction Temporal data naturally arise in many high-impact domains, including biomedicine, signal processing, meteorology, ecology, finance, prediction markets, and dynamical systems research. In these settings, knowledge of how causal relationships recur and change over time can support decisionmaking, forecasting, and intervention. In practice, temporal causal structure is rarely known priori and must be learned from data (Glymour et al., 2019). However, many advancements in statistics and machine learning assume independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables and some form of stationarity (Hastie et al., 2009), complicating their direct application to temporal data with autocorrelation and distribution shift (Figure 1). Such challenges motivate the design of special methods for time series analysis (Brockwell and Davis, 2009), including temporal causal discovery algorithms (Assaad et al., 2022; Runge et al., 2023; Hasan et al., 2023). This work considers the problem of temporal causal discovery under distribution shift. We restrict our attention to the constraint-based paradigm, which uses sequential conditional independence (CI) tests to infer graphical structure (Spirtes et al., 2001). This paradigm benefits from wealth of theoretical results, minimal innate parametric assumptions, and explainability. However, constraint-based discovery suffers from several drawbacks in the general case, including high computational complexity and high sample complexity (Shiragur et al., 2024). Window with max lag = 2 The computational complexity of constraintbased discovery is often measured with respect to (wrt) the worst-case number of CI tests required (Spirtes et al., 2001). For the general case, this is exponential wrt some graph parameter (e.g., total nodes, maximum in-degree, etc.). Unless assumptions are placed on the data generating process, it has been shown that the number of CI tests is lower bounded by value that is exponential in the maximum undirected clique size of the essential graph (Mones et al., 2026). CI testing is known to be hard problem in the general case (Shah and Peters, 2020), with exponential sample complexity wrt the size of the conditioning set. Exponential time and sample complexity can prevent tractable discovery on large data, motivating diverse strategies for pruning CI tests and reducing their order (i.e., the number of variables in the conditioning set) (Shiragur et al., 2024; Kim and Lee, 2026). We extend this effort to the time series setting, where high-dimensional data often arise. The search space of time series directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) can be significantly reduced by leveraging known problem structure, such as temporal structural priors or other graph parameters. Exploiting structural priors for efficiency gains is common strategy in local causal discovery algorithms that only learn contextually relevant subgraphs (Maasch et al., 2024). This work applies lessons from local structure learning to time series whose causal graphs are nonstationary. As an inspiration point, we naively apply previously introduced local discovery algorithms (Tsamardinos et al., 2003b; Maasch et al., 2025) in iterative fashion to obtain the global graph. As these local discovery algorithms were not intended for global time series discovery, this naive approach can entail extraneous CI tests or unnecessarily large conditioning sets. To mitigate this, we introduce an iterative procedure that is tailored for nonstationary temporal graphs. Figure 1: Full time graph with autocorrelation and causal nonstationarity. Under the false assumption that can be represented by stationary window graph with maximum lag of 2, values at time > 3 would be incorrectly forecasted. Contributions Our methodological and empirical contributions are as follows. 4 Local-to-global temporal causal discovery algorithms. 4.2 Iterative Parent Discovery on Leaves (IPaDL). We present Algorithm B.2, sound and complete naive baseline that extends previously introduced local parent discovery algorithm to the nonstationary time series setting. We use the inefficiencies of this simplistic adaptation as an inspiration and departure point for our core algorithmic contribution. 4.3 Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD). We present Algorithm 1, sound and complete causal discovery algorithm for nonstationary time series designed to reduce reliance on high-order CI tests. Additionally, we provide support for manually-derived theoretical results via AI-assisted autoformalization in Lean. 5 Empirical validation and open code. Theoretical claims are numerically verified on synthetic and semi-synthetic data. ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier wrt F1 and wall-clock time as well as F1 and unique CI tests per variable. On graphs with 1000 to 2000 variables, ITPD was the fastest running method tested. Related Works Time Series Causal Discovery Diverse strategies have been proposed for learning temporal structure from data. An historically dominant approach has been Granger causality and its variants (Granger, 1969; Geweke, 1982), including neural Granger causality (Marcinkeviˇcs and Vogt, 2021; Tank et al., 2022; Lowe et al., 2022). Constraint-based algorithms have been extended to this setting, including FCI (Entner and Hoyer, 2010). Most notably, the PCMCI family of algorithms extends PC to causally stationary settings under causal sufficiency and latent variables, with and without contemporaneous links (Runge et al., 2019; Runge, 2020; Gunther et al., 2023; Runge et al., 2023). Methods that assume functional causal models (Fujiwara et al., 2023) and neural methods also abound (Pamfil et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023). See Assaad et al. (2022); Hasan et al. (2023) for thorough surveys on time series causal discovery. Local Causal Discovery Often, the problem setting for causal discovery does not necessitate knowledge of the full graphical structure. Instead, learning local substructures is often sufficient to answer the scientific questions of interest. This emphasis on tailored local discovery can yield more computationally and sample efficient search procedures. Hence, local causal discovery (Cooper, 1997) is popular strategy for many problems, including parent and child discovery (Gao and Ji, 2015), Markov blanket (MB) discovery (Tsamardinos et al., 2003a,b; Aliferis et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014), valid adjustment set discovery (Cheng et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023; Maasch et al., 2024, 2025; Li et al., 2026), identifying necessary and sufficient explanatory variables (Cai et al., 2023), and causal fairness analysis (Maasch et al., 2025). Local learning can also be used as subroutine for global causal discovery in static DAGs (Hiremath et al., 2024) and in the time series setting (Fujiwara et al., 2023), as we do in the present work. 3. Local-to-Global Time Series Discovery This section introduces two algorithms: (1) IPaDL, sound and complete yet naive extension of an existing parent discovery algorithm (Maasch et al., 2025), which served as an inspiration point and cheap baseline for this work; and (2) ITPD, sound and complete constraint-based procedure that overcomes some of the inefficiencies of IPaDL. To handle causal nonstationarity, ITPD does not assume recurring window graph as done in baselines PCMCI (Runge et al., 2019) and DYNOTEARS (Pamfil et al., 2020), and instead learns the unique parent set for every node individually. Naive Causal Partitioning Baseline This work was inspired by the premise that one could iteratively run an efficient local parent discovery procedure to obtain global nonstationary graph. To this end, we devised naive baseline method against which to compare our final algorithm: Iterative Parent Discovery on Leaves (IPaDL; Algorithm B.2). Based on subroutine of the local causal partitioning algorithm LD3 (Maasch et al., 2024) that we term Parent Discovery on Leaves (PaDL, pronounced paddle; Algorithm B.1), IPaDL extends to the TiMINo setting for S1 and S2. Though sound and complete under sufficient conditions (Theorem 13), PaDL was designed for setting with different structural priors: namely, no time-indexing and unknown relation between and . Thus, naively applying PaDL to each variable results in extraneous CI tests and unnecessarily large conditioning sets. IPaDL therefore serves as proof-of-concept that iterative local parent discovery is viable strategy for temporal graph learning, but thoughtful extensions are required for efficiency. See Appendix for complete discussion with proofs. To our knowledge, this work represents the first case of leveraging local causal partitioning for time series discovery. Additionally, this work uses causal partitioning as convenient proof structure for proving soundness by cases. 4.3. While IPaDL is based purely on causal partitioning (Maasch et al., 2024), ITPD adopts combined strategy to reduce reliance on higher-order CI tests. ITPD exploits (1) structural priors concerning temporal order and autocorrelation, (2) causal partitioning, and (3) the local Markov condition (Definition 3). METHOD DESCRIPTION Data Settings The experimental results and main contributions of this work revolve around setting S2. The main difference between S1 and S2 is the data pre-processing performed prior to running ITPD. Namely, data corresponding to single trajectory assumed to be stationary with maximum lag τmax can be sliced and stacked to obtain trajectories of length τmax + 1. Phase II reduces this superset to strictly return the parent set. Let denote and denote t+1, where we aim to discover the parents of . We initialize the candidate set to be known parent per A1 (Line 5).
